LatentTriad:
Pre-Action Risk Representations
for Malicious Agent Skill Detection

Zhe Yu Affiliation:  The Hong Kong University of Science and Technology (Guangzhou)    Yi Liu Affiliation:  Griffith University    Ying Zhang Affiliation:  Wake Forest University    Simin Chen Affiliation:  George Mason University*Corresponding author
Abstract

Large language model agents are increasingly extended with reusable skills, but untrusted skill content can induce operations outside the user’s task. Detecting this contextual risk requires more than suspicious-pattern matching, while dynamic analysis incurs the cost of skill execution. We find that hidden states formed during prefill contain readable information about task–operation consistency, including across held-out expression forms in controlled evaluations. Matched Operation-state interventions also affect later Boundary states and shift fixed risk readouts toward the donor label. Based on these findings, we introduce LatentTriad, which combines contextual Boundary features, group-adjusted Operation directions, and departures from benign state relationships. All branches share one prefill: detection generates no output tokens, invokes no tools, and executes no skill code. Across 5,830 skill packages from five sources and seven backbones, LatentTriad achieves 99.0–99.2% pooled F1 and 93.0–94.6% source-macro F1. A separately measured compact implementation completes prefill and detection in a median of 259–284 ms. These results connect pre-action risk readability and functional influence to execution-free skill screening.

1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly extended with reusable skills: packages of instructions, scripts, and configurations that provide specialized capabilities. Public skill ecosystems are already large; for example, SkillsMP indexes over 3.18 million public SKILL.md files. However, loading untrusted skills also creates a security risk: their instructions and executable components can steer an agent toward operations that violate the user’s trusted task.

Detecting such behavior is difficult because skill risk is context-dependent and may be distributed across multiple components. Instructions, scripts, and configurations that appear benign in isolation may jointly induce an unauthorized operation, while sensitive operations such as file or network access can be legitimate when required by the task. Static rules based on keywords or code patterns therefore struggle to capture behavioral intent. Dynamic analysis provides stronger behavioral evidence, but requires generation, sandbox execution, and runtime monitoring, making it expensive for large-scale screening.

This raises a central question: can malicious behavior be detected after the model has interpreted a skill, but before it generates or executes an action?

We find that hidden states formed during prefill already contain information useful for determining whether a prospective operation is consistent with the trusted task. This information remains predictive when the same behavior is expressed in unseen forms. Moreover, controlled state interventions show that changing representations associated with skill operations can alter later model states and risk predictions. These results suggest that pre-action representations provide a useful middle ground between surface-level static inspection and costly execution-based analysis.

Based on these findings, we introduce LatentTriad, a pre-action detector that probes hidden representations while an agent processes the trusted task and candidate skill. From one prefill, a Boundary branch reads the complete context, an Operation branch projects operational states onto learned risk directions, and a Geometry branch measures departures from benign relationships among the skill’s stated purpose, operations, and context. LatentTriad generates no output tokens, invokes no tools, and executes no skill-provided code.

We evaluate LatentTriad on 5,830 skill packages from five source datasets across seven model backbones. LatentTriad achieves 99.0–99.2% pooled F1 and 93.0–94.6% source-macro F1. Cross-form evaluations show that risk information generalizes to unseen expressions, while controlled interventions show that changing Operation states can affect later representations and risk-related decisions. Separately, a compact configuration completes prefill and detection in 259–284 ms median latency, compared with approximately 153 s per skill reported by the sandbox-based SkillDetonate.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    We identify task-conditioned risk information in pre-action hidden states. Controlled cross-form tests establish its readability, while matched state interventions show effects on later states and fixed risk readouts.

  • •

    We introduce LatentTriad, combining a contextual Boundary readout, group-adjusted Operation risk directions, and Geometry residuals against benign reference maps. All three branches share one prefill.

  • •

    We evaluate LatentTriad on 5,830 skill packages from five source datasets across seven backbones, achieving 99.0–99.2% pooled F1 and 93.0–94.6% source-macro F1. Source-holdout and composition studies test how detection changes across ecosystems and task-dependent skill combinations.

2 Background, Related Work and Threat Model

Agent Security. LLM agents face jailbreaks that seek to bypass safeguards and prompt injections that redirect behavior through untrusted content. Defenses act at different stages: CaMeL separates control and data flows and enforces tool-use policies (Debenedetti et al., 2025); Attention Tracker detects injections through attention patterns (Hung et al., 2024); and AgentLens monitors and intervenes on hidden representations during execution (Luo et al., 2026). Studies of refusal (Arditi et al., 2024) and Circuit Breakers (Zou et al., 2024) further connect internal representations to safety-related behavior.

Agent Skills. An agent skill packages a root SKILL.md with optional scripts, configuration, and auxiliary resources. The host exposes names and descriptions for selection, then loads the selected skill’s instructions. The agent may subsequently read referenced files or invoke bundled scripts. Instructions can specify a report upload, for example, with a script implementing the transfer and configuration providing its destination.

Skill Security. Table 1 compares representative skill detectors. SkillSieve combines rules, code-structure checks, and LLM-based content analysis (Hou and Yang, 2026). RouteGuard aggregates response-conditioned signals from repeated fixed-continuation probes over SKILL.md, excluding auxiliary files (Xiao et al., 2026). SkillDetonate checks sandbox behavior against configured security policies (Ji et al., 2026).

Our setting combines task-aware assessment with multi-file inspection. The trusted task establishes authorization, while instructions, scripts, and configuration jointly specify the requested operations. We inspect the assembled package in that context, retaining evidence from its components.

For example, a backup task can authorize reading project files and writing to an approved directory. A script that uploads those files to a destination supplied by configuration crosses that boundary, even if the declaration still promises a local backup. The detector needs the task, script, and destination together; the declaration supplies a claim, not authorization.

We study evidence available after the model processes this input but before generation or execution. Section 3 examines its risk information; Section 4 constructs the detector.

Threat Model. The attacker controls the skill package and seeks operations outside the trusted task, including credential exfiltration or unauthorized file changes. They may distribute or obscure content across files, but cannot alter trusted prompts, model weights, runtime hooks, or detector labels. The defender controls prompt assembly and action permissions and has white-box access to hidden states. It screens the loaded input before generation or tool use. The runtime enforces the verdict, since textual refusal does not guarantee tool-call safety (Cartagena and Teixeira, 2026). Effects revealed only by later downloads or environmental interactions require runtime checks.

3 Risk Information in Pre-Action Representations

We test whether prefill states provide task-aware risk evidence: can it transfer across expression forms, affect later computation, and provide information beyond the final state? The controlled studies below motivate the readouts in Section 4.

Declaration, Operation, and Boundary States. The Declaration describes the skill’s stated purpose. The Operation contains its operational instructions, scripts, configuration, and readable auxiliary content. The Boundary is the final prompt position after the complete task and skill, before generation. We mean-pool the designated Declaration and Operation regions to obtain D and O, and sample the final position to obtain B.

For input xx, let 𝒟⁡(x)\mathcal{D}(x) and 𝒪⁡(x)\mathcal{O}(x) denote the token positions assigned to Declaration and Operation, and let TT denote the final prompt-token position. At layer ℓ\ell,

𝐡ℓD=meant∈𝒟⁡(x)⁡𝐡ℓ,t,𝐡ℓO=meant∈𝒪⁡(x)⁡𝐡ℓ,t,𝐡ℓB=𝐡ℓ,T.\mathbf{h}^{D}_{\ell}=\operatorname{mean}_{t\in\mathcal{D}(x)}\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t},\qquad\mathbf{h}^{O}_{\ell}=\operatorname{mean}_{t\in\mathcal{O}(x)}\mathbf{h}_{\ell,t},\qquad\mathbf{h}^{B}_{\ell}=\mathbf{h}_{\ell,T}. (1)

For package detection, D covers the root front matter, title, and first prose section; O covers the remaining root text and readable auxiliary files. These label-independent masks follow document structure, so O includes prose as well as code. B denotes a sampling position, not an authorization variable. Extraction and mask-sensitivity tests appear in Appendices A.1 and G.3.

3.1 Risk Information Generalizes Across Expression Forms

The same operation can be authorized by one task and forbidden by another. We test whether readouts recover this relation beyond its surface form.

The study uses 800 task–operation examples across ten domains and four forms: natural language, Python, JSON, and mixed text. Five domain-grouped folds keep related variants together. We fit compact 32-dimensional D, O, and B diagnostic readouts (fixing probe capacity to isolate representational content across depths without overfitting) on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3 without test data. Each held-out form is absent from both training and development, and its test examples also come from held-out domains. This separates transfer to a new expression form from recognizing variants seen during fitting.

O and B carry risk information at different depths. On Llama, O becomes predictive earlier but weakens at later layers; B remains highly predictive (illustrated conceptually in Figure 2a; measured AUROC across depth in Figure 3). With all forms in training, B and O reach 98.86–100.00% out-of-fold AUROC, while Declaration, TF-IDF, and length controls remain near chance. Holding each test form out of training and development leaves Boundary AUROC at 90.09–100.00% (Appendix Table 32). Risk remains readable even when form changes dominate whole-vector distances, motivating learned readouts rather than raw distance thresholds.

The states are contextual representations from the assembled input, not embeddings of independently encoded fragments. Near-chance D prediction in this controlled study does not make the declaration irrelevant: its stated purpose can still provide a reference for interpreting operational content. The different O and B trajectories instead show why a single endpoint need not expose every predictive direction equally well.

3.2 Operation States Affect Later Computation

Readability alone does not establish downstream influence. We replace O using donors matched on domain, task, compatibility rule, and expression form, with only the operation object changed. Frozen diagnostic logits move toward the donor label by 2.376–2.909 across three backbones. This diagnostic reads O directly; a separate one-layer protocol measures later B states (Appendices G.2 and E.3).

The controls distinguish a matched risk change from replacing a state at all: sham replacement, norm-matched noise, unrelated Declaration perturbations, and mismatched donors test position, magnitude, and semantic matching. Restoring B after the diagnostic intervention leaves most of its effect intact, consistent with that diagnostic’s direct access to O. The later-state experiment therefore supplies a separate test of downstream influence.

Recovery measures the patch-induced B displacement along the donor direction, normalized by the donor–recipient separation. O-only replacement yields median normalized B recovery of 0.592 on Llama and 0.944 on Qwen (Figure 2b). A separate compact multi-depth test produces 34.5–66.1 percentage points more pass-to-block flips than matched controls across seven backbones on threshold-eligible pairs (Appendix Table 29).

These results confirm that replacing operational states causally shifts downstream boundary representations in the donor direction, establishing downstream influence and justifying an operation-level readout alongside the contextual endpoint.

3.3 Combining Multiple States Can Provide Additional Information

To compare multi-state and B-only readouts, we fix the bytes of three skill files and vary their connections and authorization across 4,608 presentations in five domain-grouped folds. In this setup, skills form a multi-step chain where intermediate outputs route between files (e.g., Skill 1 →\to Skill 2 →\to Skill 3; Appendix Figure 6a); the workspace configures connections and a starting key, determining an end target verified by a deterministic no-I/O oracle against the authorization policy. This changes the risk relation purely through compositional routing without introducing new file content. Individual-node and partial-context controls remain near chance. Multi-state readouts reach 68.5–75.2% authorization-pair accuracy, versus 48.8–53.8% for B-only (Appendix Figure 6b; Appendix G.5). The constructed multi-state features therefore outperform the tested B-only readout. Matched-capacity controls further distinguish multi-state features from the smaller, backbone-dependent gain of explicit residuals. Because the readouts also differ in feature construction and width, this comparison establishes the usefulness of the constructed multi-state features, rather than isolating access to an additional state. The capacity-matched package controls in Section 6.2 test the narrower contribution of residual construction.

Extracting D, O, and B within a single prefill provides complementary local and contextual risk evidence without separate component encodings, directly motivating the tripartite readout architecture in Section 4. Section 6.2 tests the resulting feature and policy choices on skill packages.

4 LatentTriad

LatentTriad converts the evidence in Section 3 into package-level risk scores (Figure 1). Boundary reads the complete context, Operation measures learned risk contrasts, and Geometry compares state relationships with benign references. The branches share one frozen-model prefill; a fixed policy combines their scores before generation or skill execution.

4.1 Input Assembly and State Extraction

The runtime serializes the trusted prompt, task, tool schema, and multi-file skill package in deterministic path order, preserving file boundaries. One prefill extracts the states in Equation 1 at eight fixed normalized depths and retains individual D/O spans for local features. All branches and their three member encoders reuse these tensors. Appendix A.1 specifies the input and extraction contract. Pooling supplies a package-level view; retained spans preserve local content that may be brief relative to the full package. Both views come from the same contextual computation, so local feature extraction adds no model generation or second prefill.

4.2 Complementary Risk Readouts

Each branch fits three member encoders on different family-grouped training partitions. We omit the member index below.

Boundary. Boundary reads the raw B state at a depth selected on non-test data. It retains contextual evidence without constructing cross-region residuals.

Operation. The Operation branch isolates operational risk directions by reducing domain- and family-specific stylistic variations that could confound classification. To perform this group adjustment, training families are partitioned into five artificial strata (distinct from source ecosystems). At each depth, class means of normalized O states define a local risk contrast within each stratum, and directions fitted to stratum centroids are projected out to remove fitted between-stratum directions. Projections onto these adjusted contrasts and their mean direction are pooled across eight depths into a standardized feature vector (Appendix A.2). Supervised package heads thus read operational risk from adjusted risk contrasts rather than raw between-stratum variation.

Geometry. The Geometry branch captures the relational alignment characteristic of benign skills—where stated intent (DD), concrete operations (OO), and task context (BB) exhibit consistent mappings—and evaluates departures from fitted benign reference relationships. Normalized states enter shared 32-dimensional coordinates 𝐳ℓR,a\mathbf{z}^{R,a}_{\ell} fitted on benign packages for relations a∈{D​O,O​B}a\in\{DO,OB\}. Each member fits affine ridge maps TℓaT^{a}_{\ell} on benign packages to predict expected operational states from declarations (D→OD\to O) and context from operations (O→BO\to B):

𝐫ℓD​O\displaystyle\mathbf{r}^{DO}_{\ell} =𝐳O,D​Oℓ−TD​Oℓ(𝐳D,D​Oℓ),𝐫O​Bℓ=𝐳B,O​Bℓ−TO​Bℓ(𝐳O,O​Bℓ).\displaystyle=\mathbf{z}^{O,DO}_{\ell}-T^{DO}_{\ell}(\mathbf{z}^{D,DO}_{\ell}),\qquad\mathbf{r}^{OB}_{\ell}=\mathbf{z}^{B,OB}_{\ell}-T^{OB}_{\ell}(\mathbf{z}^{O,OB}_{\ell}). (2)

These observed-minus-predicted residuals measure structural deviations from fitted benign references rather than causal mappings. Crucially, residual magnitude alone does not constitute an independent anomaly verdict; rather, a supervised head learns which directional departures and structural discrepancies correlate with actual risk. In addition to pooled residuals, matching each individual O span to its nearest predicted counterpart retains brief payloads that global pooling might dilute. Features summarize residual vectors, layer-wise evolution, and multi-depth alignment, which are subsequently mapped to calibrated package-level predictions (Appendix A.2).

4.3 Training and Pre-Action Decision

For each Large-ID split, a standardized L2-logistic head maps the concatenated member features ϕq\bm{\phi}_{q} to a branch probability:

pq​(x)=σ⁡(𝐰q⊤​Std⁡(ϕq​(x))+cq),q∈{boundary,operation,geometry}.p_{q}(x)=\sigma\!\left(\mathbf{w}_{q}^{\top}\operatorname{Std}(\bm{\phi}_{q}(x))+c_{q}\right),\quad q\in\{\mathrm{boundary},\mathrm{operation},\mathrm{geometry}\}. (3)

Encoders use training packages only; final heads use training and development packages. Test packages are excluded from fitting and selection.

Boundary risk is sufficient to block; an additional Operation-triggered block requires Geometry support:

s⁡(x)=max⁡{pboundary​(x),min⁡(poperation​(x),pgeometry​(x))}.s(x)=\max\!\left\{p_{\mathrm{boundary}}(x),\min\!\left(p_{\mathrm{operation}}(x),p_{\mathrm{geometry}}(x)\right)\right\}. (4)

This fixed, interpretable policy applies the threshold rule

verdict⁡(x)={block,s⁡(x)≥0.5,pass,s⁡(x)<0.5.\operatorname{verdict}(x)=\begin{cases}\text{{block}},&s(x)\geq 0.5,\\ \text{{pass}},&s(x)<0.5.\end{cases} (5)

Geometry therefore filters additional Operation alerts; it cannot block independently. Section 6.2 separates branch quality from this policy’s effects and compares simpler alternatives.

Optional risk-localization heads reuse D/O states without affecting the verdict (Appendix E.2).

5 Experiments

We evaluate the Section 4 detector on seven backbones with a 24,576-token input limit. Package-level partitions and heads are fitted separately from the diagnostic studies in Section 3.

We construct Large-ID from five sources, including MalSkillBench (Guo et al., 2026), with 5,830 skills forming 2,915 source-matched malicious–benign pairs (Table 6). Families, shared documents, and paired skills form 1,954 content-linked components assigned to five source-stratified folds. Each split uses three folds for training, one for development, and one for testing. Every skill is tested once; all methods share test IDs (Appendix A.3).

Baselines. We compare LatentTriad with AgentLens, RouteGuard, and five input-level baselines on the same folds. AgentLens follows its released probe protocol; RouteGuard is reimplemented from its paper specification (Luo et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026). Selection uses development data only; Appendix B.1 specifies all implementations. The input-level baselines are Regex, SkillSieve L1, Cisco AI Skill Scanner, an LLM judge, and a supervised Qwen text readout. SkillSieve L1 is its rule stage, not the full LLM-assisted cascade.

Metrics. We report malicious-class F1, false-positive rate (FPR), AUROC, and average precision (AP). Pooled metrics weight packages equally; source-macro metrics weight sources equally. Large-ID confidence intervals use 2,000 source-stratified component-bootstrap draws. Controlled studies resample domains or families.

Controlled composition uses scenario/persona-disjoint folds, with fusion and thresholds selected on development data. Intervention and robustness studies use separate pair- or scenario-disjoint protocols, detailed with their results and in Appendices B.2–B.3.

6 Results

6.1 LatentTriad Detects Malicious Skill Packages

LatentTriad reaches 93.0–94.6% source-macro F1 across seven backbones (Table 2). Its mean of 93.9% exceeds RouteGuard’s 79.2% and AgentLens’s 62.3%; all 14 paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero. Pooled F1 is 99.0–99.2%, and source-macro AUROC and AP exceed RouteGuard on every backbone.

Pooled FPR is 1.1–1.4%; source-macro FPR is 8.0–11.2%, versus RouteGuard’s 12.9–17.9%. Equal-source reporting exposes errors masked by the 89.9% share of benign packages from one source (Appendix C.1). Among input-level baselines, the LLM judge reaches 30.5% source-macro F1 at 2.4% pooled FPR, the supervised Qwen text readout reaches 58.4% at 7.5% pooled FPR, and SkillSieve L1 reaches 60.5% source-macro F1. The same-backbone comparisons show that LatentTriad’s advantage also extends to the tested detectors using internal model signals.

To separate operation risk from surface appearance, a balanced 2×22\times 2 diagnostic varies the two factors, with 57 packages per cell. LatentTriad ranks the malicious operation above its benign counterpart in 94.7% of Llama pairs and 100% of Qwen pairs; RouteGuard ties every pair (Appendix E.1).

The component-disjoint evaluation above retains examples from every source in training. Holding out an entire source reduces mean source-macro F1 to 73.2% and AUROC to 80.3%. F1 remains above same-backbone RouteGuard and AgentLens on all seven backbones, with all 14 paired intervals excluding zero (Appendix Tables 20–21). The detection advantage transfers, but within-ecosystem performance does not.

6.2 Complementary Roles of the Three Branches

The layerwise readouts show that Operation and Boundary risk representations emerge with distinct depth dynamics (Figure 3). In the Large-ID component study under the same folds and threshold 0.5 (Table 3), adding the Operation–Geometry gate to Boundary increases recall from 92.58% to 96.73% and F1 from 91.63% to 93.91%, at the same mean FPR. Replacing Geometry with independent-state features lowers full-system AUROC by 0.076 percentage points (95% CI [0.027, 0.136]). This control retains the three states, feature dimension, and head class. Its competitive performance separates the gain of the constructed multi-state features over Boundary-only from the smaller ranking increment of explicit benign-reference residuals.

Geometry-only yields higher AUROC (99.68%) and F1 (95.85%) than Full, with zero observed FPR but lower recall (92.42% versus 96.73%). Full permits Boundary to block without Geometry agreement, increasing recall while introducing false alarms. max⁡(B,O)\max(B,O) improves recall to 97.05% at the same observed FPR and has higher F1 and AUROC, supported by paired contrasts (Appendix C.2). The fixed gate is therefore not the best policy on the reported metrics. Geometry-only is a single branch, but not a single-state baseline: its features already depend on D, O, and B. Its performance supports the multi-state feature design without establishing that all three risk heads are necessary. The stronger max⁡(B,O)\max(B,O) working point further separates access to multiple states from their final fusion. Deployment should select among these policies on independent development data according to its recall and false-alarm requirements.

6.3 Composition and Adversarial Rewrites

Compositional Attacks. We test detection under multi-skill interactions using CompoSkill’s 690 matched attack–clean pairs, which share installed skill packages but differ in cross-file execution flow. With development-selected fusion and thresholds, LatentTriad detects 93.0–97.2% of attacks at 3.8–4.3% FPR across five backbones (Appendix Table 9). These results show that pre-action readouts can detect task-conditioned compositional attacks under the tested protocol.

Adversarial Rewrites. We assess robustness against adaptive evasion across two adversarial settings. In a feedback-guided test with seven iterative rewrite rounds, detection on original execution paths remains resilient at 92.9–97.1%. Valid rewrites covering nine initially blocked Llama paths and eight Qwen paths produce only one and zero new evasions within candidate coverage (Appendix Table 13). In a white-box panel using cross-file payload splitting, attacks achieve 11.0% equal-source success on Llama, but the rewrites simultaneously increase benign FPR from 32.3–40.8% to 49.3–80.4% on that panel’s eligible subset (Appendix D.1).

Generalization Limits. To isolate structural reasoning from surface correlation, we examine workspace controls and synthetic generalization. Workspace-only TF-IDF and hidden states already perform strongly on CompoSkill (Appendix Figure 6c), indicating that benchmark cues can facilitate path detection. Conversely, under a synthetic stress test with permuted symbol assignments, performance drops to near-chance (49.25–53.47% AUROC across known and held-out templates; Appendix G.6). This divergence underscores that while LatentTriad detects many of the tested compositional attack paths, these results do not establish general structural reasoning; rather, detection relies on contextualized representations rather than abstract cross-file symbol interpretation.

Request-Level Containment. Finally, we evaluate runtime mediation in a 256-pair broker simulation. Under a 30% containment budget, LatentTriad achieves 17.2% attack success and 46.7% valid benign allowance averaged across seven backbones (Appendix Table 24). The broker records candidate request decisions without executing payloads, illustrating practical enforcement trade-offs.

6.4 Runtime Cost

To characterize the cost of pre-action screening, we measure a compact detector configuration in a high-throughput setting. Employing 8/24 D/O spans and member-level CDF scoring, this compact configuration adds only 56–65 ms on Llama and Qwen, yielding a median prefill-plus-detection latency of 259–284 ms for this specific variant (Appendix Table 31). In contrast, the full Large-ID detector prioritizes detection fidelity using 8/256 spans and concatenated logistic heads; its end-to-end runtime is not directly measured and should not be extrapolated from this compact measurement. Both variants share one prefill across branches without generating tokens. The measured increment covers state collection, feature construction, and scoring; Appendix F specifies the timing boundaries.

7 Conclusion

We investigate risk assessment before action generation or execution. Controlled studies show that prefill states contain readable task-conditioned risk information across expression forms, while Operation-state interventions affect later representations and fixed risk readouts. Building on these findings, LatentTriad combines contextual, operational, and relational evidence for execution-free skill screening through one prefill. Evaluations across five sources and seven backbones demonstrate its detection value under the tested conditions. Pre-action screening complements execution-time permission enforcement and runtime monitoring.

AI Use Statement

Generative AI assistants supported code implementation and debugging, experiment orchestration, figure and table preparation, and language editing. The authors defined the research questions and evaluation protocols, reviewed the experimental artifacts, and take responsibility for the reported results, claims, and conclusions.

Ethics Statement

This work handles malicious-skill artifacts that could inform evasion. Experiments run in isolated environments without external credentials or unrestricted network access. Released examples will redact credentials and live endpoints, minimize executable harm, and retain only the structure needed to reproduce detector measurements. We report false positives because blocking benign skills is also an operational harm. Dataset use and redistribution remain subject to the licenses and terms of their original sources.

Reproducibility Statement

The method, prompt and extraction contract, threat model, split construction, model-selection protocol, and evaluation metrics are specified in Sections 4 and 5. The appendix records the extraction settings, baseline specifications, statistical procedures, and data-use conditions. The anonymous repository11 1 https://anonymous.4open.science/r/latenttriad-review-5FDB/ provides the method implementation and reference configurations. Its manifests/ directory records sample and pair IDs, group-aware splits, eligibility and exclusion records, and frozen source revisions.

Appendix A Reproducibility and Data Contracts

This section specifies the serialized prompt, region map, backbone, fitted representation, split, and threshold needed to reproduce the score and verdict from a package tree. Package detection, intervention, and runtime measurements use the settings in Table 30. Controlled representation studies specify their diagnostic readouts separately in Appendix G.

A.1 Exact Runtime and Input Contract

Hidden states depend on the input contract: changing the serializer, chat template, or tool schema can change the representation of the same package.

Pre-action endpoint.

The detector runs after the complete skill package enters the protected model’s context. It finishes before the model generates a token, selects a tool, or causes an external side effect. The detector observes the native prefill that loads the task, tool interface, and skill. It executes no package content and exposes no labels, analyst rationales, or future outcomes to the model.

Prompt and tool contract.

The frozen system message is specified in Box A.1. The available interface contains one function, run_shell, with one required string field, cmd. The user message and package subtree follow the exact serialization template shown in Box A.2. This formatting is fixed across classes, sources, methods, and backbones.

⬇
// 1. Tool Declaration (Native Function Schema)
{
”name”: ”run_shell”,
”description”: ”Execute a shell command within the protected workspace environment.”,
”parameters”: {
”type”: ”object”,
”properties”: {
”cmd”: {”type”: ”string”, ”description”: ”Shell command to run.”}
},
”required”: [”cmd”]
}
}
// 2. Serialized Input Structure
<trusted_user_task>
{task}
</trusted_user_task>
<loaded_skill_package
input_unit=”owning_skill_subtree”
serialization=”path_sorted_inert_static”>
<skill_file path=”SKILL.md”>
{root_declaration_and_instructions}
</skill_file>
<skill_file path=”{relative_auxiliary_file_path}”>
{auxiliary_code_or_configuration}
</skill_file>
</loaded_skill_package>

Package serialization.

An input is the owning skill subtree rooted at SKILL.md. Files are serialized in lexicographic relative-path order. Readable UTF-8 files retain their relative path and text inside skill_file delimiters. Binary files are represented by a path and placeholder. Their bytes never enter the prompt. The detector covers the root declaration, scripts, configuration, and readable auxiliary material loaded by the agent.

Region binding.

Declaration covers the root front matter, title, and first prose section. Operation covers the remainder of the root file plus all readable auxiliary text. The binding uses package structure as a proxy for semantic role: O can include prose, examples, and configuration as well as executable code. Boundary is the native assistant-generation suffix, or the implicit prompt end immediately before generation or tool selection. Character spans are projected to model-native token offsets. A token crossing a region boundary is assigned to exactly one region. D and O must both be nonempty. Large-ID and its white-box panel retain at most eight Declaration atoms and 256 Operation atoms. The compact intervention and CDF-consensus timing configurations retain eight and 24, respectively. Atom limits belong to the extraction configuration, not to the definition of D/O; each comparison holds them fixed across classes and backbones.

Eligibility and failure behavior.

Large-ID uses a 24,576-token cap and the balanced 2×22\times 2 uses 12,288. Each protocol defines its own support. These caps are not model-specific truncation settings. A package enters a cross-backbone comparison only when every included tokenizer preserves every required region. Missing root files, ambiguous or empty spans, removed required content, incompatible model or prompt contracts, and nonfinite features produce an explicit contract error. The pipeline never silently truncates a required region or treats a contract failure as benign. Changes to the backbone, tokenizer, prompt, tool schema, or region map require revalidation before reusing fitted readouts.

A.2 Complete Detector Algorithm

The following steps specify the default package-level policy. CompoSkill’s development-only adaptation is described in Appendix B.2.

Inputs and outputs.

Inputs are a trusted task, a tool schema, a serialized skill subtree, the protected backbone, the D/O/B representation bundle, and three component readouts. The decision threshold is 0.5. Outputs are a continuous risk score, three branch probabilities, a binary pass/block decision, and coverage status.

Inference procedure.

The end-to-end detection flow for each skill package is formalized in Algorithm A.1. All three ensemble members reuse the same prefill tensors, forming an efficient statistical ensemble without additional model executions.

Large-ID fitting partitions.

The package detector uses three outer training folds, one development fold, and one test fold. Training family identifiers are sorted and assigned round-robin to five artificial strata. These strata govern inner partitioning, Boundary-depth selection, Operation directions, and Geometry reference weighting; they are not ecosystem labels. For each offset j∈{300,400,500}j\in\{300,400,500\}, the first split of a five-way stratified grouped partition gives inner fit and calibration sets, using seed 20260802+1000+j20260802+1000+j. The grouping unit is the content-linked component described in Appendix A.3.

Each member fits candidate Boundary probes on inner-fit packages. On the calibration set, a cutoff limits empirical FPR to at most 5% in each artificial stratum. We select depth by stratum-macro F1, breaking ties by AUROC and then shallower depth. Only the selected depth is retained: its raw hidden vector enters the final Boundary matrix, not the candidate probe’s score or cutoff. Three members therefore contribute 3​d3d Boundary coordinates for hidden width dd.

Operation encoder.

At each depth, unit-normalized O vectors define a benign and malicious mean within each inner-fit stratum. The midpoint of these two class means is the stratum centroid. We center by the mean of the five centroids and remove at most two nondegenerate right-singular directions of their centered matrix. Each stratum’s malicious-minus-benign contrast is projected out of this same subspace and unit-normalized. Write n⁡(𝐯)=𝐯/max⁡(‖𝐯‖2,10−8)n(\mathbf{v})=\mathbf{v}/\max(\|\mathbf{v}\|_{2},10^{-8}), let 𝝁ℓ,s+\bm{\mu}_{\ell,s}^{+} and 𝝁ℓ,s−\bm{\mu}_{\ell,s}^{-} denote the class means, and let 𝐜ℓ\mathbf{c}_{\ell} be the mean stratum centroid. The columns of UℓU_{\ell} contain the retained singular directions. Then

Πℓ\displaystyle\Pi_{\ell} =I−Uℓ​Uℓ⊤,\displaystyle=I-U_{\ell}U_{\ell}^{\top}, 𝐯ℓ,s\displaystyle\mathbf{v}_{\ell,s} =n⁡(Πℓ​(𝝁ℓ,s+−𝝁ℓ,s−)),\displaystyle=n\!\left(\Pi_{\ell}(\bm{\mu}_{\ell,s}^{+}-\bm{\mu}_{\ell,s}^{-})\right), (6)

At inference, O vectors are first unit-normalized, then centered, projected out of the fitted subspace, and dotted with the contrasts, without a second normalization. Five values summarize each depth: the projection onto their normalized mean direction and the mean, minimum, maximum, and standard deviation of individual contrast projections. We retain all eight depth values and four trajectory summaries (mean, standard deviation, maximum, and late-half minus early-half mean), giving 5​(8+4)=605(8+4)=60 features per member and 180 in the concatenated Operation matrix. The encoder retains all 180 features after removing stratum-centroid directions.

Geometry coordinates and transport.

Two shared 32-dimensional projections use all benign outer-training packages, with equal package weights. At each depth, D and O are individually unit-normalized; the mean of their paired means defines a common center. The leading right-singular vectors of the stacked centered D/O vectors define PℓD​OP^{DO}_{\ell}. O/B independently define PℓO​BP^{OB}_{\ell} by the same procedure. Projection seeds are 20260822 and 20260922, respectively, plus the layer position. For relation a∈{D​O,O​B}a\in\{DO,OB\}, common center 𝝁ℓa\bm{\mu}^{a}_{\ell}, and shared projection PℓaP^{a}_{\ell}, the coordinates are

𝐳ℓR,a=Pℓa​(n⁡(𝐡ℓR)−𝝁ℓa).\mathbf{z}^{R,a}_{\ell}=P^{a}_{\ell}\big(n(\mathbf{h}^{R}_{\ell})-\bm{\mu}^{a}_{\ell}\big). (7)

Equation 7 applies to pooled states and individual atoms, using ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8}. D, O, B, and D/O atoms enter D/O coordinates; O and B also enter O/B coordinates. Projected arrays are stored in float16. Transport and residual arithmetic use float32; the B-norm denominator in the relative O/B residual is computed from its stored float16 array. Angular gaps below are 1−cos⁡(⋅,⋅)1-\cos(\cdot,\cdot); norm denominators are floored at ϵ\epsilon.

Within each member’s inner-fit set, affine ridge maps Tℓa​(𝐳)=Wℓa​𝐳+𝐛ℓaT^{a}_{\ell}(\mathbf{z})=W^{a}_{\ell}\mathbf{z}+\mathbf{b}^{a}_{\ell} with regularization 1.0 and an unpenalized intercept fit benign D→\rightarrowO and O→\rightarrowB pairs, giving each artificial stratum equal total weight. For each O atom, we select the nearest transported D atom by Euclidean distance in D/O coordinates and retain their residual. The layer’s local threshold is the median of the five strata’s benign 90th-percentile atom distances. Only benign Large-ID training packages fit these projections, maps, and thresholds.

Geometry feature matrix.

Each depth contributes eight D→\rightarrowO features: the mean, 75th and 90th percentiles, maximum, and standard deviation of atom distances; the fraction exceeding the local threshold; the pooled transport residual norm; and the angular gap between predicted and observed O. Let 𝐮ℓ\mathbf{u}_{\ell} be the mean atom residual weighted by positive distance exceedance, with uniform valid-atom weights when total exceedance is at most ϵ\epsilon. Each of the three resulting feature blocks adds its mean, standard deviation, maximum, and 90th percentile across the expanded block coordinates (12 values).
