Thus each member supplies 228+12+5=245228+12+5=245 Geometry features, or 735 after concatenation. Geometry undergoes neither Operation-style stratum-subspace removal nor feature selection.

Only the final standardizers and C=1C=1 L2-logistic readouts use outer training plus development, without class weighting or feature selection. Equation 4 fuses their probabilities directly at cutoff 0.5; this Large-ID readout has no empirical-CDF calibration.

A.3 Dataset Construction and Study Scope

The following tables identify the data used for detector fitting, mechanism analysis, and evaluation. Studies that reuse a dataset retain their stated training and test partitions.

Source releases and pairing.

Table 6 links each source to its frozen revision. We construct benign–malicious pairs within each source, preferring available controls from the same upstream family. Remaining controls are matched one-to-one by package size and total, text, and binary file counts. The support manifest retains source revisions, sample IDs, pair IDs, and matching modes for each package.

Evaluation groups.

Package detection joins original groups, shared-content links, and benign–malicious pair links into connected components. The resulting 1,954 components partition all 5,830 packages into five folds. Shared document and package identities stay within one fold even when a matched pair contains different package trees. Components define both fitting partitions and bootstrap units.

All learned methods in Table 2 use these components. White-box, multi-depth intervention, and broker tests instead use application probes fitted on matched-pair-disjoint folds. Their folds keep each constructed pair together but do not enforce separation of all shared-content components. These probes remain fixed during each application test. Localization and composed-skill studies use their stated family and role-group partitions. Ecosystem labels support matching and evaluation, not runtime detection.

Splits and counterfactual selection.

Splits are fixed before any method is fit. Trainable methods finalize their parameters and operating point before each test fold. The balanced 2×22\times 2 contains 57 packages in each combination of benign/suspicious surface and benign/malicious operation. Candidate inverse groups first satisfy dual-model token eligibility and pair completeness. A deterministic content-based ordering then selects groups without labels, model outputs, or detector scores.

Safety of data handling.

All studies use inert package loading. Scripts and auxiliary payloads are serialized as model input but are not executed. No evaluation grants package code credentials, unrestricted network access, or a writable production environment.

A.4 Malicious-Package Composition

Malicious packages vary in both behavior and presentation. For the three locally available Large-ID sources, we inspect complete owning subtrees, including root instructions and any available scripts, references, configuration, or self-check material. ATR Skill Benchmark and SkillsBench-1650 use their source taxonomies and labels. Their files remain sealed.

Three properties make detection difficult. Semantic dilution hides a small unsafe clause inside a long, useful package. Relational violation makes each local step plausible even when the declaration, implementation, recipient, permission, or self-check disagrees. Representation opacity delays meaning until encoded content, binaries, network responses, or runtime branches are decoded or executed. LatentTriad targets relational violation and can also expose some semantic dilution. Representation opacity requires sandboxing or runtime monitoring.

Appendix B Baselines and Statistical Protocol

Baselines differ in their inputs and fitting procedures. We specify both below so that comparisons can be interpreted in context.

Adjacent threats and defenses.

Position-aware skill injection and threshold sharing across tools make harmful instructions less conspicuous (Hao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026a). Input defenses can remove suspected instructions (Shi et al., 2025). Attention Tracker detects injection through attention patterns (Hung et al., 2024), whereas Rennervate provides token-level detection and sanitization (Zhong et al., 2025). ProbGuard predicts future violations from runtime traces (Wang et al., 2025). These systems motivate separate comparisons for package surface, model state, and execution state.

B.1 Baseline Contracts

Static control.

Static Regex applies a suspicious-operation pattern set, requires no fit, and does not read protected-model states. Its backbone-independent result appears once in the shared panel of each detection table.

Released scanners and semantic judge.

SkillSieve L1 uses the released deterministic first-stage parser/scanner. Cisco AI Skill Scanner uses the official implementation22 2 https://github.com/cisco-ai-defense/skill-scanner, the default ScanPolicy, and its static, bytecode, and pipeline analyzers. Its native is_safe decision blocks Critical or High findings. Ordinal maximum severity supplies AUROC and AP. No package code is executed. On Large-ID, the strict loader accepts 5,577 packages. The documented lenient loader handles 253 packages with missing or malformed frontmatter, preserving all 5,830 common IDs.

LLM-as-judge renders the same package to a frozen Mistral-7B model and compares benign/malicious verbalizer likelihoods without generation (Box B.1). It cannot access the protected model’s hidden state. The supervised text readout scores the rendered package with Qwen2.5-7B. It uses two full-package verbalizer log-likelihoods as inputs to a standardizer and C=1C=1 L2-logistic classifier. The classifier fits on each Large-ID training-plus-development partition and uses threshold 0.5. Test labels select no feature, parameter, or operating point.

Internal baselines.

RouteGuard is a paper-spec reimplementation of attention/hidden-state fusion with four probe prefills. AgentLens learns interpretable safety-steering representations from coding-agent trajectories. We transfer its released probe protocol to the loaded-skill pre-action Boundary as specified below.

Selection fairness.

Fairness means identical test IDs, family partitions, and decision timing, not identical training code. In Large-ID, LatentTriad refits projections and member encoders on training families. RouteGuard refits its four probes on training data. AgentLens uses development to select layer and epoch before a training-plus-development refit. LatentTriad and the supervised text baseline fit their readouts on training plus development without selecting an operating point. AgentLens retains its published argmax rule. RouteGuard and LatentTriad use the same 0.5 probability decision. No method receives a test label, per-source threshold, or post-hoc target recall.

AgentLens task transfer.

We extract the full Boundary last-token vector and fix the layer range to the released training script’s default first 28 layers across backbones.33 3 Release: AgentLens@22d397d0. A group-disjoint development partition selects the layer and epoch. The probe preserves the released AgentLens optimization contract: Linear(h,2)(h,2) plus softmax, Adam with learning rate 10−210^{-2}, cross-entropy loss, batch size 16, and at most 100 epochs. It adds no standardization, sample weighting, Top-K detection, or ensemble. The selected probe is refit on training plus development and evaluated once with its argmax decision.

On deeper backbones, this fixed layer range differs from LatentTriad’s full-depth grid. The methods also differ in member construction and readout adaptation. Appendix C.2 uses the final Large-ID fits to separate fusion, relation features, and member construction. A dimension-matched independent-state control replaces Geometry while retaining the B/O heads; single-member controls refit the readouts for each retained member.

B.2 Compositional Path Calibration

CompoSkill Path uses the same extracted states for the fixed and nested LatentTriad variants. The fixed contract applies max⁡(B,min⁡(O,G))\max(B,\min(O,G)) at threshold 0.5. The nested contract changes only the fusion rule and operating point. Each fold fits heads on training data, selects one of four monotone rules and 33 thresholds by development equal-threat macro F1, and then refits the heads on training plus development. The outer test fold is evaluated once. The candidate rules and thresholds are specified before evaluation; the fixed policy serves as a separate control.

B.3 Compositional Mechanism and Adaptive Stress

Table 11 reports explicit and implicit attack modes derived from CompoSkill-Bench (Liu et al., 2026b). We freeze dataset revision 1a13cca244 4 Full revision: https://huggingface.co/datasets/Limax11/CompoSkill-Bench/tree/1a13cca2a63c9d6fdcc196df853c3a372ed31e8a.. Its primary design contains 380 three-skill instances, each with clean, explicit, and implicit variants (1,140 records). We pair each available attack variant with its clean counterpart, requiring a valid task, a resolved source–bridge–terminal chain, and complete workspace files. Implicit variants also require a valid execution guide, matching path length, and no primary-chain skill identifiers in the sanitized payload. Missing variants are not synthesized. This yields 344 explicit and 346 implicit pairs (690 mode-specific pairs, 1,380 evaluation rows); a clean variant can appear in both modes. The five outer folds separate scenario/persona role groups. LatentTriad and AgentLens use one native prefill; RouteGuard uses four fixed probe prefills. Cisco Cross-Skill uses the official scanner to jointly inspect the three installed root documents. Our root-document adaptation of SkillReact extracts capability conjunctions from those documents; the original framework also inspects bundled code (Wang et al., 2026). Our Qwen3-30B-A3B reimplementation of ChainGuard evaluates each candidate against previously installed skills, following ColluSkill’s context-aware procedure (Zeng et al., 2026).

The serialized path includes the trusted task, the root SKILL.md of each active skill in path order, and the workspace visible at the audited boundary. In this path-specific region map, D contains the task and skill declarations; unlike the package map, it includes the trusted task. O contains the remaining skill instructions and visible workspace. Auxiliary package files remain tool-addressable but are not loaded into this path view. Private JSON keys beginning with an underscore are removed recursively from implicit execution guides; labels and attack-mode metadata are also excluded. The explicit view precedes chain execution. The implicit view follows workspace observation and precedes the terminal action. Both are single-prefill inspections of a given path context, rather than end-to-end planner rollouts.

Table 9 pools all 690 mode-specific pairs to report original-path detection and the seven-round stress endpoint on the same support. It covers five backbones, including Llama-3.3-70B in INT8; the path inputs, fold protocol, and development-only selection rules are unchanged. Table 11 instead pools paths within each mode separately for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B. LatentTriad reaches 88.5–99.9% F1 and 0.0–8.7% FPR across the four backbone–mode cells. Three paired F1 gains over RouteGuard exclude zero; the Llama explicit gain is 1.2 points [-1.4, 3.9]. The installation checks receive identical skill documents for both members of each pair, without the task or workspace that distinguishes their risk.

Node-only scanners answer a narrower question: whether independent package inspection can recover a risk that emerges only from composition. They inspect each activated package separately and never observe the complete task path.

The SCR-Bench panel (Xie et al., 2026) transfers the fitted CompoSkill detectors without using an SCR label for fitting or threshold selection. It contains 667 matched cases: 150 capability-flow, 401 trust-transfer, and 116 authorization-confusion pairs. We use source revision b8bb3e9e.55 5 Release: SCR-Bench@b8bb3e9e. Of its 118 AuthBlur cases, authblur:26 and authblur:76 lack the plain-advisor variant required for the four-condition panel, leaving 116 eligible cases. Primary contrasts are terminal-only versus composed-neutral for capability flow, control versus experiment for trust transfer, and level 0 versus level 3 for authorization confusion. Each pair holds the case and downstream action fixed while changing the mechanism condition. We use 2,000 case-paired bootstrap draws and 20,000 paired sign-flip draws. Holm correction is applied across the three mechanisms within each backbone and method.

The adaptive panel adapts ColluSkill’s scanner-feedback rewriting to our path-level detector (Zeng et al., 2026). We generate candidates over seven rounds. At each round, the attacker receives the verdict, branch scores, and high-risk region summary. A candidate must preserve the task, node order, tools, paths, endpoints, artifact handoffs, and capability graph. It must also pass an independent frozen semantic judge. All 690 original paths remain in the denominator, and path-paired uncertainty uses 2,000 bootstrap draws. Invalid rewrites retain the preceding valid path and never count as successful attacks. The rewrites target LatentTriad; AgentLens and RouteGuard score the same resulting paths, rather than candidates optimized separately against each baseline.

Table 13 separates detector performance from attack coverage for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B. Of the initially blocked paths, nine on Llama-3.1-8B and eight on Qwen2.5-7B receive at least one valid rewrite. These sets contain nine distinct mode-specific paths in total. New evasions occur on one of Llama’s nine paths and none of Qwen’s eight. Repeated rounds on the same path do not increase this coverage. The evasion rate over all paths reflects both the attacker’s ability to produce valid candidates and the detector’s response. Conditional rates on these nine and eight paths isolate the response to valid rewrites.

B.4 Metrics, Aggregation, and Statistical Inference

Pooled metrics describe the observed package mixture; source-macro metrics give each ecosystem equal influence.

For malicious as the positive class, we compute

FPR=FPFP+TN,FNR=FNFN+TP,\mathrm{FPR}=\frac{\mathrm{FP}}{\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{TN}},\quad\mathrm{FNR}=\frac{\mathrm{FN}}{\mathrm{FN}+\mathrm{TP}},
Precision=TPTP+FP,Recall=TPTP+FN,F1=2​T​P2​T​P+FP+FN.\mathrm{Precision}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}},\quad\mathrm{Recall}=\frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}},\quad\mathrm{F1}=\frac{2\mathrm{TP}}{2\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}+\mathrm{FN}}.

Undefined precision is set to zero when a method predicts no positives. For Skill detection, each learned method is fitted independently on each split. We pool predictions from the five nonoverlapping test folds. Source-macro metrics are computed within each source and then averaged equally over the five sources. If source ss has ns−n_{s}^{-} benign packages,

FPRpooled=∑sFPs∑sns−,FPRsource=15​∑sFPsns−.\mathrm{FPR}_{\mathrm{pooled}}=\frac{\sum_{s}\mathrm{FP}_{s}}{\sum_{s}n_{s}^{-}},\qquad\mathrm{FPR}_{\mathrm{source}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{s}\frac{\mathrm{FP}_{s}}{n_{s}^{-}}.

The former weights source-specific FPR by benign sample counts; the latter assigns each source 20%. Both retain every test package. An expected deployment FPR would instead use the source proportions among benign deployment requests. Confidence intervals use 2,000 shared bootstrap replicates. Components are stratified by their source-membership sets and resampled with replacement. Each draw includes all packages in the selected components for every method. We then recompute source-macro F1. The 14 LatentTriad-minus-comparator intervals share these draws, preserving component, source, method, and backbone pairing. These are per-comparison 95% intervals, not multiplicity-adjusted tests.

The five-source LOSO protocol performs five additional refits per learned method. Each refit withholds one ecosystem from fitting, development selection, and calibration. We compute metrics on each held-out source and average the five results. The 2,000 paired replicates resample matched families within the held-out source. Every method and backbone receives the same family multiplicities.

Average precision is the step-integrated area under the precision–recall curve. At each distinct score, precision is weighted by the increase in recall. We compute AP from sample-level ranking scores. Aggregate confusion counts are insufficient. Cisco contributes its discrete ordinal severity instead of a calibrated probability. AUROC is threshold-independent; it is the primary metric for the final-configuration relation-feature contrast and a ranking diagnostic elsewhere. PairAcc is the fraction of matched inverse pairs in which the malicious-operation member receives the higher risk score. A tie contributes one half. We use PairAcc only for matched counterfactual diagnostics.

Appendix C Large-ID Detection and Cross-Source Generalization

Source slices, component controls, and paired contrasts use the same component-disjoint package detector. Source-holdout evaluation fits separate detectors with the test ecosystem excluded.

C.1 Source-Wise and Paired Results

Table 6 shows the source imbalance. MalSkillBench supplies 2,621 of the 2,915 benign packages (89.9%). LatentTriad’s FPR on this source is 0.5–0.8% across backbones; on SkillFortify, it is 0%. Rates are higher on the other three sources, which contain 114 benign packages in total (Table 15). For example, Llama flags 17/2,621 MalSkillBench packages, 0/180 SkillFortify packages, 10/63 SkillsBench1650 packages, 1/29 Agent-skill malware packages, and 5/22 ATR packages. This gives a pooled FPR of 33/2,915 (1.13%) and a source-macro FPR of 8.54%. The latter weights each source equally, exposing differences in benign acceptance that the dominant source would otherwise mask.

Table 14 reports source-wise F1, and Table 16 gives all same-backbone contrasts and confidence intervals.

C.2 Final-Configuration Component Controls

These controls use the component-disjoint Large-ID configuration in Table 2 (summarized in main-text Table 3): seven backbones, five folds, eight depths, and three members with offsets 300, 400, and 500. These are follow-up controls on the same folds; their results do not select the reported detector.

The first comparison fixes all fitted component scores and varies only the fusion: BB, OO, GG, max⁡(B,O)\max(B,O), min⁡(O,G)\min(O,G), or the full rule. All use threshold 0.5. The second replaces Geometry with independent-state features while retaining B/O scores, input coverage, member partitions, head family, and fusion. For each member, D and O concatenate pooled projected states and atom-coordinate means, standard deviations, and maximum absolute values across eight depths. B concatenates its eight O→\rightarrowB-projected states. Separate unwhitened PCA fits on benign member-training rows retain 82 D, 82 O, and 81 B coordinates. Concatenating the three members gives 735 features. The replacement Geometry head uses the same standardizer and L2 logistic readout (C=1C=1), fit on training plus development. This control contains no cross-region residuals, differences, distances, or dot products.

The third comparison refits all three branch heads for each original member separately, using the same training recipe. We report all three members and the arithmetic mean of their metrics, rather than selecting the best member or averaging their scores. Three-member concatenation changes feature width as well as member count. The equal-width Geometry control matches input dimension and head family, not every aspect of statistical capacity.

For each backbone, metrics are computed on the concatenated out-of-fold predictions, then averaged equally over sources. Table 17 averages these metrics over the seven fixed backbones. Table 19 retains the backbone-level results. The combined branches complement Boundary-only: Full raises mean recall from 92.58% to 96.73% and F1 from 91.63% to 93.91%. Both flag exactly the same benign packages on each backbone, giving 9.51% mean FPR. Explicit relation features add 0.076 points of AUROC over the equal-width independent-state control. All seven point estimates are positive.

The remaining controls distinguish this complementarity from the choice of fusion rule. Geometry-only yields 95.85% F1 and 92.42% recall with no false alarms. At threshold 0.5, it trades lower recall than Full for higher F1 on these data. Zero observed FPR describes this fitted operating point, not a guarantee on new traffic. The simpler max⁡(B,O)\max(B,O) rule reaches 94.08% F1 and 97.05% recall at the same FPR as Full. Here, Geometry confirmation removes some true alarms from that rule without removing false alarms. These results support the multi-state evidence, but do not identify the full rule as the best operating point.

Three members differ from the single-member mean by 0.032 AUROC points, 0.029 AP points, and 0.340 F1 points. All three intervals include zero (Table 18), so this comparison does not establish a mean ensemble gain.

The primary contrast is the seven-backbone mean source-macro AUROC difference between Full and the independent-state control. Its 95% interval is [0.027, 0.136] percentage points. We use 2,000 paired component-bootstrap draws, stratified by source-membership signature, with shared component multiplicities across methods, members, and backbones. Every draw recomputes AUROC and AP from the saved scores, including ties. Intervals use the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles and are conditional on the fitted models. A two-sided test with 5,000 shared component-level method swaps gives raw p=0.00020p=0.00020; seed 20260910 fixes both procedures. The intervals in Table 18 are pointwise.

C.3 Five-Source Large-ID Leave-One-Source-Out Evaluation

With the complete test ecosystem withheld from fitting, LatentTriad retains meaningful detection performance, although it falls below within-ecosystem results. It averages 73.2% source-macro F1 and 80.3% AUROC, retaining higher F1 than same-backbone RouteGuard and AgentLens on all seven backbones (all 14 paired bootstrap intervals exclude zero). Recall and AP average 76.6% and 82.0%. Tables 20 and 21 give the aggregate results and paired representation contrasts with 2,000-draw bootstrap confidence intervals.

The advantage is metric-dependent. The supervised Qwen text readout has lower F1 (58.7%) but higher AUROC (88.1%) and AP (90.0%). LatentTriad therefore leads the same-backbone representation monitors in F1, not every comparator on every metric. Its mean F1 also exceeds the 66.7% positive-class F1 of an all-positive rule, which has 100% FPR on the source-balanced data. Deployment still requires measuring recall and false alarms at the chosen operating point; F1 alone does not establish a cold-start alert budget.

Appendix D Robustness and Enforcement Results

The white-box and broker studies use the pair-disjoint application probes defined in Appendix A.3. They measure rewrite sensitivity and request-level containment with the probes held fixed.

D.1 White-Box Adversarial Robustness

The panel asks whether an attacker can manipulate visible D/O/B geometry while preserving the original operation. It contains 256 family-unique matched pairs from all five Large-ID sources. Source quotas are set by the evaluation protocol. Eligible package roots are at most 16,384 bytes and admit a safe Operation newline split. Each pair contributes clean, region-padding, cross-file-split, and six Geometry-candidate views. This yields 4,608 package views per backbone. The attacker knows the native tokenizer, D/O/B binding, fold-specific detector bundle, fusion, and threshold. It may rewrite package documentation and layout before capability loading, but it cannot modify model or detector parameters. Geometry evasion chooses the lowest Geometry-margin candidate from the malicious package alone. We then apply the same candidate index to its matched benign control.

The three candidate rewrite mechanisms are detailed in Box D.1. Exact deletion or ordered concatenation reconstructs every original package. Every original non-root file is byte-identical, and no original operation byte is deleted. No package content is executed.

Every view is scored by the detector fitted for its original Large-ID test fold, without refitting or a threshold change. The inference unit is the matched family, and metrics average the five sources equally. Intervals use 2,000 source-stratified family-bootstrap draws. Fused and Geometry logit-margin shifts use 10,000 source-stratified family sign flips. We apply separate Holm corrections across the 21 backbone–attack tests. The robustness criterion requires at least 80% TPR retention and an empirical-bootstrap 95% upper endpoint of at most 25% for attack success.

In Table 23, Δ​m\Delta m is the attacked-minus-clean fused logit margin, without percentage scaling. pH​(m)p_{\mathrm{H}}(m) and pH​(mG)p_{\mathrm{H}}(m_{G}) test fused and Geometry margin shifts, respectively.

TPR retention is the attacked source-macro TPR divided by the clean source-macro TPR, expressed as a percentage. It can exceed 100% when rewriting makes previously missed attacks detectable. ASR first divides successful pass-after-rewrite evasions by clean true positives within each source, then averages the defined source rates. Thus its denominator is the clean-detected subset of the 256 malicious packages, not all package views. Benign FPR uses the 256 matched benign packages with equal source weighting. When no evasion is observed, every bootstrap replicate also contains zero evasions, producing [0,0][0,0]. This interval reflects the observed sample; it does not bound the population evasion rate at zero.

For a zero-event cell with nsn_{s} clean true positives in source ss, a source-wise binomial model gives the one-sided upper endpoint us=1−(0.05/5)1/nsu_{s}=1-(0.05/5)^{1/n_{s}}. Bonferroni coverage then yields the conservative 95% upper bound Umacro=15​∑susU_{\mathrm{macro}}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{s}u_{s}. Table 22 reports the eight zero-event cells using their actual source denominators. These bounds assume independent Bernoulli family trials with a common evasion probability within each source, conditional on clean detection, the selected support, and the tested rewrite. They require no independence across sources and apply per cell, not simultaneously across all 21 cells. Dependence between content-linked families (Appendix A.3) remains outside that model.

The supplementary bounds span 11.90–12.48%. The table below also reports empirical-bootstrap intervals for all cells; the binomial bounds apply only to zero-event cells.

All 21 backbone–attack cells satisfy this empirical anti-evasion criterion. Cross-file splitting is the strongest attack. Its equal-source ASR reaches 11.0% [6.5, 16.3] on Llama, while TPR retention remains at least 92.3% on Qwen2.5-7B. Region padding and Geometry search achieve TPR retention of at least 101.6% and 100.7%, respectively. Geometry-search ASR is at most 3.1%. The selected rewrite changes the Geometry margin in 19/21 cells after Holm correction, but these changes rarely produce successful evasion. Manipulating one exposed component therefore does not imply control of the fused verdict.

The matched benign controls expose a different cost: the attacks raise alert load even when they rarely evade detection. Clean equal-source FPR is 32.3–40.8% on this length- and split-eligible subset and becomes 49.3–80.4% after the same inert rewrites. This panel therefore measures both evasion resistance and the benign interruption cost of the fixed rule. Canonicalization and alert-budget calibration are deployment choices to evaluate against that cost, not validated mitigations in this panel.

D.2 Capability-Broker Enforcement

This experiment measures request-level policy enforcement on 256 family-unique matched safe–unsafe pairs from all five ecosystems. Sample selection uses neither detector scores nor acting-model outputs. Each of the seven protected models loads the complete package through its native chat and tool template. It then encodes the candidate operation as one typed request_capability action (Box D.2). The schema requires scope, destination, authorization, and persistence arguments. Malformed requests fail closed.

⬇
{
”action”: ”request_capability”,
”arguments”: {
”scope”: ”filesystem” | ”network” | ”subprocess” | ”credentials”,
”destination”: ”<target_file_path | remote_endpoint_url>”,
”authorization”: ”<policy_token | user_confirmation | none>”,
”persistence”: true | false
}
}

A policy-independent parser records each request before applying a policy. AgentLens, RouteGuard, and LatentTriad route the same recorded requests using their package scores under 10, 20, and 30% containment budgets. Only the routing score changes. The inert broker records allow or contain; even allow executes no package payload, generated command, or network request. All models use greedy decoding. Qwen3 disables its optional reasoning trace for this deterministic typed-encoding task. Confidence intervals use 10,000 paired bootstrap draws over source-stratified operation pairs.

Let VV indicate a parser-valid typed request, UU an unsafe argument combination, and CC selection for score-based containment. The categorical checker marks unrelated or private resources, unapproved or private destinations, absent or bypassed authorization, persistence, and unknown values as unsafe. For the budgeted policies, allowance is A=V⁡(1−C)A=V(1-C). This Boolean allowance is request allowance, not payload execution. For package label yy, the reported endpoints are

ASR=∑y=1V​U​ANunsafe,BenignRequestAllowance=∑y=0V⁡(1−U)​ANsafe.\mathrm{ASR}=\frac{\sum_{y=1}VUA}{N_{\mathrm{unsafe}}},\qquad\mathrm{BenignRequestAllowance}=\frac{\sum_{y=0}V(1-U)A}{N_{\mathrm{safe}}}.

Here Nunsafe=Nsafe=256N_{\mathrm{unsafe}}=N_{\mathrm{safe}}=256 per acting model. Benign request allowance counts valid, checker-safe requests that the broker allows; it does not measure completion of an executed task. Request validity is ∑V/512\sum V/512; score-based policy rejection is ∑C/512\sum C/512, with malformed requests additionally contained. Conditional attack success divides the same unsafe allowance count by ∑y=1V​U\sum_{y=1}VU. The table reports the all-unsafe denominator. For paired intervention comparisons, the prevented-attack count is ∑y=1V​U​C\sum_{y=1}VUC; 1−ASR1-\mathrm{ASR} also includes invalid or non-unsafe requests and is not the broker’s blocking rate.

Table 24 averages package-level rates over seven acting models. Random averages 20 seeds; Oracle uses labels. Allow-all records 82.4% valid requests, 46.7% unsafe-request allowance, and 47.1% benign-request allowance. Against AgentLens, LatentTriad reduces unsafe-request allowance by 6.1, 9.2, and 11.0 points at the three budgets and increases benign-request allowance by 5.6, 7.5, and 8.4 points. Both metrics favor LatentTriad in a fraction 1.0 of bootstrap draws at each budget. At 30% containment, the corresponding differences from RouteGuard are −2.4-2.4 points (95% CI [−4.4,−0.4][-4.4,-0.4]) and +0.95+0.95 points ([0.22,1.67][0.22,1.67]); both metrics favor LatentTriad in a fraction 0.990 of draws.

Appendix E Operation Sensitivity and Localization

E.1 Balanced Counterfactual Diagnosis

The balanced 2×22\times 2 design crosses visible surface with operation semantics. B/B denotes benign surface and benign operation. B/M keeps the benign surface but inserts a malicious operation. S/B combines suspicious surface with benign operation, while S/M is suspicious in both dimensions. Each quadrant has 57 packages, so lexical appearance and operation labels are independently balanced.

Llama LatentTriad ranks malicious operations above their matched benign counterparts in 94.7% of pairs, and Qwen orders every pair correctly. RouteGuard ties every pair. These results separate operation-sensitive score ordering from package-surface classification. Figure 4a shows all methods and paired intervals.

E.2 Auxiliary Risk Localization

The localization experiment predicts the region containing risky content. It reuses hidden states from the same native prefill and fits two C=1C=1 L2-logistic readouts: one on Declaration features and one on Code/Operation features. Thresholding both outputs at 0.5 gives four classes: clean (0,0)(0,0), decl (1,0)(1,0), code (0,1)(0,1), and both (1,1)(1,1). These auxiliary predictions enter neither the three-branch score nor the policy threshold. The tables’ attribution labels denote content localization, not causal attribution of the primary decision.

The natural panel contains 610 packages from 150 grouped families: 210 clean, 115 decl, 175 code, and 110 both. It spans five source ecosystems and six malicious-risk categories. The controlled panel contains 128 base families, each represented by clean, Declaration-only, Code-only, and dual-region variants. All members of a family remain in one of five outer folds. The reported intervals resample families within source 2,000 times.

In Table 26, D/C denotes the Declaration and Code heads. “Blocked” counts primary-detector blocks among 400 malicious packages; conditional exact attribution measures correctness within those blocks. Joint success requires both the correct primary verdict and exact attribution among all 610 natural packages.

Because the two heads reuse cached D/O states, their median cost is 1.6–3.1 ms and their peak additional memory is below 25 MB on every backbone.

E.3 Exact-Slot O→\rightarrowB Causal Confirmation

We test whether Operation states affect the pre-action Boundary, beyond supporting a diagnostic readout. The test contains 40 source–target families. Within each family, operation slots have equal token counts and identical absolute Operation and Boundary positions under both native tokenizers. A score-blind odd/even split assigns 20 families to development and 20 to confirmation. Development selects the best of seven normalized intervention layers by its smallest mean margin over the controls (Llama layer 3 and Qwen layer 9). No confirmation family informs layer selection, controls, or gates.

At the selected layer, the exact source Operation token states replace the aligned target states. Let 𝐛t\mathbf{b}_{t}, 𝐛s\mathbf{b}_{s}, and 𝐛p\mathbf{b}_{p} denote the target, donor, and patched Boundary vectors. Recovery is the normalized projection of the patch-induced displacement onto the donor direction:

Recovery=(𝐛p−𝐛t)⊤​(𝐛s−𝐛t)‖𝐛s−𝐛t‖22+10−8.\mathrm{Recovery}=\frac{(\mathbf{b}_{p}-\mathbf{b}_{t})^{\top}(\mathbf{b}_{s}-\mathbf{b}_{t})}{\|\mathbf{b}_{s}-\mathbf{b}_{t}\|_{2}^{2}+10^{-8}}.

It measures directional displacement, not fractional distance reduction. Four controls isolate specificity: eight same-energy random directions at the same slot, the semantic delta at an equal-length neutral slot, a permutation of the source token order, and a per-token rescaled delta from another family. Confidence intervals use 10,000 paired family-bootstrap replicates.

Exact replacement produces positive Boundary recovery in all 20 confirmation families on each backbone. Llama’s median recovery is 0.592. Its mean recovery gains over the random, neutral-position, token-permutation, and mismatched-semantic controls are 0.420 [0.379, 0.457], 0.439 [0.407, 0.474], 0.323 [0.277, 0.373], and 0.219 [0.186, 0.251], respectively. Qwen’s median recovery is 0.944. Its corresponding gains are 0.743 [0.672, 0.804], 0.876 [0.823, 0.929], 0.540 [0.464, 0.613], and 0.366 [0.277, 0.451]. Every confirmation gate passes on both backbones. Replacing Operation states therefore moves the downstream Boundary toward the donor state on held-out families. This measures causal O→\rightarrowB influence; the learned transport residual is a separate statistical proxy. The following experiment measures application-probe response to multi-depth Operation interventions.

E.4 Detector-Aligned Score and Verdict Test

This experiment uses 100 distinct Large-ID matched families, with 20 pairs drawn from each source by a deterministic, score-blind rule. Every pair uses the fixed application probe for which its matched family was outer-test data. It recomputes the eight-depth input with a compact limit of eight D and 24 O atoms, reusing the Large-ID projections, member encoders, and final readouts. No head is refit and no additional ensemble is formed. The intervention starts from the benign package and inserts the matched malicious Operation trajectory at doses 0.25, 0.50, and 1.00. It patches the seven causally upstream depths of the detector’s eight-depth trajectory; the final depth is excluded because it cannot alter the same-layer Boundary state.

At each depth, Operation atoms are aligned by normalized order. Their malicious-minus-benign mean difference is added to all target-atom tokens. Two controls use independent Gaussian directions at the same atoms and depths, with every atom-level norm matched to the real intervention. We then recompute the Boundary state, the three component margins, and the fixed-threshold verdict. For component k∈{B,O,G}k\in\{B,O,G\}, the logit margin is mk=log⁡[pk/(1−pk)]m_{k}=\log[p_{k}/(1-p_{k})]. We report the fused margin

m⁡(x)=max⁡{mB​(x),min⁡(mO​(x),mG​(x))}=logit⁡s⁡(x).m(x)=\max\{m_{B}(x),\min(m_{O}(x),m_{G}(x))\}=\operatorname{logit}s(x). (8)

Thus m⁡(x)≥0m(x)\geq 0 gives the same verdict as s⁡(x)≥0.5s(x)\geq 0.5 in Equation 5. The intervention generates no tokens and executes no payload.

Point estimates weight the five sources equally. Confidence intervals use 10,000 source-stratified family-bootstrap replicates. One-sided family sign-flip tests compare the real intervention with its random controls; Holm correction is applied across seven backbones separately for each endpoint. Eligibility for the verdict analysis is fixed before intervention: the benign score must be below the operating threshold and its matched malicious score at or above it. For each pair, dose AUC is the trapezoidal integral of the real-minus-control response over doses {0,0.25,0.50,1.00}\{0,0.25,0.50,1.00\}.

Branch activity is measured on unpatched benign targets. Verdict Δ\Delta is the full-dose real-minus-random pass-to-block rate among eligible pairs.

Natural malicious-over-benign PairAcc is 86–92%. The real trajectory patch produces positive Boundary-recovery, Boundary-head, Operation-head, and fused logit-margin dose responses on all seven backbones after Holm correction (pH<10−3p_{\mathrm{H}}<10^{-3} throughout). Geometry also responds on five. The final logit-margin dose AUC ranges from 2.465 to 3.621. Depending on the backbone, 51–61 of the 100 pairs are threshold-eligible. Within this set, the real patch raises pass-to-block flips by 34.5–66.1 percentage points over the norm-matched controls; every interval excludes zero. The single-depth experiment tests O→\rightarrowB influence. The multi-depth experiment measures joint three-branch response and verdict sensitivity under compact extraction; neither isolates Boundary as the necessary mediator of the fused decision.

Appendix F Runtime and Resource Accounting

F.1 Measurement Protocol and Costs

Runtime measurements use the compact CDF-consensus configuration, rather than the package detector. Table 30 lists the extraction and scoring settings for each study.

The compact measurements use one RTX 4090 host with Python 3.12.13, PyTorch 2.6.0, CUDA 12.4, Transformers 5.13.0, BF16, SDPA, and batch size one. After 20 warmups, we measure 120 MalSkillBench packages per backbone three times with GPU synchronization. This yields 360 paired measurements per backbone. Six empirical token-length bins contribute 20 packages each. Labels and detector scores do not affect selection. Peak process GPU memory is 17,574 MiB for Llama and 17,242 MiB for Qwen.

The frozen timing benchmark subtracts a paired no-hook prefill from the instrumented forward and scoring interval. The increment includes hook callbacks, D/O/B pooling, projections, feature construction, member-level CDF calibration, and consensus scoring. Model loading, tokenization and sample preparation, bundle/projection loading, and hook registration/removal occur outside the timed interval. It aggregates Boundary and Operation member margins by their medians and Geometry by its maximum. Its 64.7 ms Llama and 56.1 ms Qwen median increments measure this compact pipeline, not the current 256-atom, concatenated-logistic Large-ID pipeline.

The capability-broker’s greedy typed-request generation is not included in detector increments. Table 31 separates native prefill from detector overhead; neither overhead alone nor the compact configuration establishes total agent latency or the full Large-ID configuration’s runtime.

Appendix G Controlled Pre-Action Representation Studies

These studies distinguish information accessible to a diagnostic readout from the performance of the deployed detector. Unless specified otherwise, the three backbones are Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, and Mistral-7B-v0.3. B32 and O32 read 32-dimensional Boundary and Operation representations, respectively. The independent-state (Ind.192) and residual-feature (Rel.192) readouts each use 192 features. They differ from the full-width Boundary and 735-dimensional Geometry components in Large-ID. These studies do not change the reported package detector or its threshold.

G.1 Risk Prediction Across Expression Forms

The controlled dataset has 800 examples from ten domain blocks, five task–operation compatibility rules, and four expression forms: natural language, Python plans, JSON configuration, and mixed text. Matched operations preserve the trusted task and vary whether the selected object satisfies its compatibility rule. Same-group variants stay together. Five folds hold out domain blocks; the all-forms condition includes every form in training and test. Each of the four leave-one-form-out conditions excludes its test form from both training and development and evaluates it on held-out domains.

All projections and benign-reference maps fit on training examples. Development selects layer, logistic regularization, and the operating threshold. Ind.192 constructs features separately from each state; Rel.192 includes benign transport residuals. B32, O32, and D32 read one region, while TF-IDF and length provide text controls. The seven methods, three models, and five settings yield 105 aggregate metric rows. Table 32 reports all settings. Each all-forms evaluation uses 800 examples; each held-out-form evaluation uses 200.

AUROC pools out-of-fold predictions from frozen heads. Intervals resample the ten domain blocks 5,000 times, keeping related variants together. Paired AUROC tests enumerate the 1,024 domain-level method-score swaps and apply Holm correction to three prespecified comparisons per model and setting. In all-forms evaluation, Rel.192 exceeds TF-IDF on all three backbones (corrected p=0.00586p=0.00586), but does not significantly exceed B32 or Ind.192. This comparison concerns the fitted lexical baseline, not every possible static analyzer.

Pairwise ordering and pooled ranking measure different properties. On many holdouts, matched-pair accuracy remains high even when pooled AUROC decreases. Score scales can differ across domains and independently fitted fold heads. For example, Mistral’s held-out Python Rel.192 readout has 67.79% pooled AUROC but 100% matched-pair accuracy. Qwen’s natural-language holdout also loses pairwise ordering, so score-scale changes do not explain every failure. These exploratory comparisons do not select a new calibration or test threshold.

Layerwise distances use training-fitted coordinate standardization. We compare a semantic-preserving form change with a risk-changing operation under fixed form. Form changes dominate whole-vector distances at most depths, despite strong risk readouts. Qwen’s late Boundary states show the opposite ordering; Llama and Mistral do not share this reversal. Pointwise domain-bootstrap intervals describe individual depths, without selecting test-set peaks or claiming simultaneous layerwise significance.

G.2 Matched Operation Interventions

For each of the 800 recipients per model, the all-forms Rel.192 diagnostic and its development threshold remain frozen. At the depth preceding the selected readout, we intervene on Operation states using a donor matched in domain, compatibility rule, expression form, and trusted task. Only the operation object changes. Both benign-to-malicious and malicious-to-benign directions are included. We report the logit-margin change directed toward the donor label, not a probability change or an attack execution rate.

Controls comprise an unchanged forward pass, a sham replacement, same-position norm-matched random perturbations, unrelated Declaration perturbations with matched total energy, norm-matched semantically mismatched donors, and the matched Operation donor followed by restoration of Boundary to its unpatched state. Five random seeds are averaged within each recipient before domain aggregation. They do not increase the independent sample count. Table 33 includes all conditions.

Matched donors flip the frozen diagnostic decision on 46.75%, 34.13%, and 28.75% of recipients on Llama, Qwen, and Mistral, respectively. All four prespecified matched-control contrasts per model pass the domain-level sign-swap test with Holm-corrected p=0.0078125p=0.0078125. Equal corrected values arise from the finite set of domain sign swaps, not equal effect sizes.

Sham effects and verdict flips are zero. Most of the matched-donor effect remains after Boundary restoration: the diagnostic still directly reads O and cross-region residuals. This supports functional sensitivity to the operation intervention without establishing Boundary as a necessary mediator. The separate exact-slot and compact detector-aligned experiments in Appendices E.3 and E.4 retain their own inputs, heads, and statistical units.

G.3 Region Masks on Identical Hidden States

D/O are structural proxies, not a natural-language/code partition. The heading parser can treat a #-prefixed line within a code fence as a heading. Across 5,830 packages, this moves the declaration boundary inside a fence in 27 cases (0.46%). We test all 27 affected cases and 27 matched controls on Llama and Qwen. The serialized input, tokens, hidden states, and Boundary state are unchanged; only the D/O pooling masks change.

Neither model changes a binary verdict on the affected cases. Maximum absolute probability changes are 0.30932 on Llama and 0.02283 on Qwen. Thus, this concrete parsing issue does not change decisions in the tested set, but some scores are sensitive to the mask. The experiment is neither a semantic segmentation accuracy estimate nor evidence that all possible region definitions are equivalent. All reported detector results use the same structural parsing rule; this test changes masks only for diagnosis.

G.4 CompoSkill Input Dependence

The monitoring set comprises 344 explicit and 346 implicit malicious–benign pairs: 690 mode-specific pairs, or 1,380 records. These are not 690 independent attack families. Their family union contains 361 identities, 329 shared between modes, grouped into 76 scenario/persona role groups. The five threat categories contribute 150 data-exfiltration, 128 memory-tampering, 140 multi-agent-hijack, 123 privilege/dangerous-command, and 149 resource-exhaustion pairs.

Input ablations refit diagnostic readouts under the same five role-group folds. They compare the task, workspace, installed nodes, local contexts, and full path, using the original labels for the full paths. A workspace-only TF-IDF readout reaches 98.38% explicit and 100.00% implicit AUROC. Pure-node views are at 50% because each matched pair has identical skill content. On Llama, a full-path diagnostic reaches 84.97/99.62% AUROC (explicit/implicit), versus 93.64/100.00% for workspace only. On Qwen, the corresponding values are 95.75/99.99% and 95.24/100.00%. These are diagnostic refits, not the final path detector.

Workspace cues therefore suffice for strong prediction on this benchmark. This does not mean that the final detector relies only on workspace cues. It means that benchmark accuracy alone cannot identify how the model represents skill dependencies. The controlled fixed-node study below tests that question without directly exposing the final target in the workspace.

G.5 Fixed-Node Composition Counterfactuals

We fix the bytes of three skill files and cross their connection and authorization settings. The workspace supplies routing and a starting key; the composed finite map determines the target. A deterministic, no-I/O oracle checks whether that target is authorized. The 144 adaptable cases and 31 domain labels are drawn from SCR-CapFlow’s organization, yielding 1,152 bundles and 4,608 four-cell presentations. This is one controlled finite-map mechanism, not 31 independent mechanisms or the original SCR-Bench attack evaluation.

Five domain-grouped folds keep related variants together. Layers and hyperparameters are selected on development. Input-deletion controls retain the original full-path labels: their chance performance indicates missing information for that label, not safety of a newly defined partial task. Table 34 includes all 19 methods.

Figure 7a contains 186 comparisons: three backbones, 31 domains, and two multi-state readouts. Panel b compares the two 192-dimensional readouts on the same 93 backbone–domain pairs; B32 uses 32 dimensions. For panel c, each backbone contributes 2,304 authorization pairs. The empirical distributions weight backbones and domains equally and retain all held-out pairs. A positive score difference ranks the unauthorized input higher; magnitudes are not calibrated across readouts. Panels share inputs, not independent replicates.

Figure 8 separates the paired responses by backbone. Each panel retains all 2,304 held-out authorization pairs for each multi-state readout, without jitter or filtering. The two readouts share pairs, yielding 13,824 plotted points rather than independent experimental replicates. The diagonal indicates equal numerical score differences, not equivalent calibration across heads.

Independent-state and residual features both use squared transformations and 192 dimensions. Relative to the independent construction, residual AUROC changes by −5.86-5.86 [−7.77-7.77, −3.92-3.92] points on Llama, +1.92+1.92 [−1.45-1.45, +5.23+5.23] on Qwen, and +8.82+8.82 [+7.08+7.08, +10.51+10.51] on Mistral. Holm-corrected paired pp values are 0.00080, 0.27275, and 0.00080. The residual contribution therefore depends on the backbone. Comparisons with B32 change feature width and construction as well as the regions read. Using squared features in a readout does not identify a particular nonlinear computation inside the model.

The corresponding composition intervention uses all 4,608 recipients per model, half with changed risk and half with unchanged risk. Matched workspace donors keep skill files and the trusted task fixed. Donor-directed diagnostic margin changes are 0.172/0.292/0.154 for Llama/Qwen/Mistral, versus 0.002/−0.0001-0.0001/−0.0005-0.0005 for norm-matched random controls and 0.069/0.084/0.044 for mismatched donors. Restoring B leaves 0.172/0.288/0.158. However, unchanged-risk recipients still flip decisions at 14.92/7.06/8.47%, compared with 14.31/6.85/2.02% on changed-risk recipients. The intervention changes the diagnostic but does not isolate a risk-specific causal effect. It therefore does not establish a universal composition mechanism.

G.6 Full-Architecture Structural Transfer

The broader synthetic test uses six templates: dictionary binding, role requirements, credential validation, delegation chains, scope intersection, and conditional fallback. Each model has 2,304 inputs: 576 training, 192 development, and 1,536 test presentations. The test uses new opaque symbol assignments, with both single-skill and composed packaging and two neutral-edit variants. The known-template panel trains on all six templates. Six leave-one-template-out panels train on 480 and develop on 160 examples, testing 256 presentations of the omitted template. Template reuse and symbol changes define the generalization axis; these are not independent natural attack mechanisms.

Unlike the pooled diagnostic readouts, this test fits the complete LatentTriad architecture from genuine local atoms at eight depths. It retains 32-dimensional latent coordinates, offsets 300/400/500, the unmodified component-head family, and fixed max–min fusion. The models run in BF16 without quantization, CPU offload, or truncation. Four state-feature controls, Boundary-only, and LatentTriad are evaluated on every panel. Independent-linear here is fitted on synthetic training data, whereas the independent-state control in Appendix C.2 is fitted on natural packages.

Table 35 reports all 96 aggregate AUROC cells. Ind.L and Ind.S use independent linear and squared features; Orth.S uses orthogonal squared features; Quad. uses explicit quadratic features. Held-out entries are means of all six template panels, not pooled scores from different fitted heads. We provide descriptive results without treating six constructed templates as a population of independent mechanisms.

For the main neutral variant, LatentTriad AUROC ranges from 49.25% to 53.47%. At both development-calibrated 5% and 10% FPR budgets, LatentTriad and Boundary-only make identical test decisions on every panel and packaging. This identity also holds for the second neutral variant. Development-budget calibration does not ensure the same test FPR: at the 10% budget, test FPR is 3.12–9.38% in known-template panels but 28.65–34.38% under template holdout. This test therefore supports neither stable structural transfer nor a low-FPR advantage over Boundary-only. It refits the architecture on synthetic training data; it does not reevaluate the natural-package checkpoints.

The finite-map result and this broader transfer test answer different questions. Retaining local atoms at eight depths does not recover transfer here, so missing local features alone cannot explain the result.

G.7 Same-Prompt Readouts and Generated Judgments

This exploratory program test uses three operators (object flow, delegation, and conditional selection), six lexical families, four expression forms, two packaging styles, and both answer orders. Each model has four condition–target panels of 384 questions: the actual object must either be inferred or is supplied, and the target is either the object or its risk. Three operator folds rotate training, development, and test roles. Actual-object and risk heads are trained separately. All three fixed seeds reuse the same questions, so they do not triple the independent support.

For each question, the Boundary readout and generation start from the exact same prompt. The readout uses the first prefill; generation is evaluated at 96, 256, and 512 tokens. Bfull uses the model’s full hidden width rather than a compressed B32/B128 projection. The table reports all fixed methods, including random-training-label and text controls. Development chooses regularization from {0.01,0.1,1}\{0.01,0.1,1\}, with ties resolved toward smaller values.

Random denotes the B128 random-training-label control; Text uses the full question and Options removes the program. Format failures are counted as errors rather than discarded. In particular, Qwen’s inferred-risk accuracy rises from 23.18% at 96 tokens to 94.53% at 512 tokens, with format failures falling from 286 to 2. A short-budget failure is not evidence that the model cannot solve the task.

Bfull inferred-risk accuracy is 53.39% on Llama and 53.12% on Qwen, compared with 76.56% and 94.53% after 512-token generation. Supplying the actual object raises Bfull to 59.90% and 89.84%. This separates successful generated reasoning from accessibility to the tested fixed linear head. It does not prove that the first prefill lacks the information, that generation creates new knowledge, or that model scale determines detectability.

Appendix H Discussion and Limitations

H.1 Scope of Pre-Action Risk Readability

Pre-action readouts expose a different capability from generated judgments. On inferred-object prompts, Qwen reaches 94.53% risk-answer accuracy with a 512-token generation budget, versus 53.12% for a full-width linear Boundary readout on the same prompts (Appendix G.7). Supplying the actual operation object raises that Boundary readout to 89.84%. For this probe, reading an explicit task–operation relation is easier than first resolving the operation from an implicit composition. The contrast concerns accessibility to the tested linear head, not the absence of information from the first prefill or generation creating new knowledge.

The intervention protocols also answer distinct questions. A diagnostic that reads O directly can respond to its replacement even when B is restored. The exact-slot experiment measures downstream B displacement, while the compact detector-aligned experiment measures frozen score and verdict changes. These tests establish functional effects in their respective settings; they do not establish B as a necessary mediator or measure an agent’s execution of the patched operation (Appendices G.2, E.3, and E.4).

H.2 Generalization Beyond Training Distributions

Expression, ecosystem, and structural shifts change different parts of the problem. Held-out-form prediction tests new expressions of the controlled task–operation relations, with domains also held out. Source holdout changes the skill ecosystem and reduces performance despite an advantage over the tested baselines (Section 6.1). Expression transfer therefore supports robustness to the tested forms, not ecosystem-independent screening.

The fixed-node study changes connections and authorization while keeping file bytes fixed. Its multi-state features outperform the tested B-only readout, but the comparison also changes feature width and construction. The broader synthetic study refits the full architecture under new symbol assignments and remains near chance even on known templates (Appendix G.6); it does not reevaluate the natural-package checkpoints. This is a broader inference requirement than decoding an explicit operation’s task consistency. Likewise, strong workspace-only controls on CompoSkill show that benchmark accuracy alone cannot identify which dependency information a detector uses.

H.3 Deployment and Runtime Boundaries

Deployment should select readouts, thresholds, and fusion on independent development data for its detection objective. Geometry-only has the strongest observed F1 and zero observed FPR in the component panel, whereas max⁡(B,O)\max(B,O) improves recall, F1, and AUROC over the fixed max–min rule at the same displayed FPR. These comparisons distinguish the representation design from the choice of decision policy. The reported fixed rule remains unchanged; deployment-specific operating points require separate selection rather than choosing a new policy from test outcomes. Zero observed false positives in this panel is not a guarantee for future traffic.

The detector requires white-box access and the input contract in Appendix A.1. It can inspect only content available in the loaded context. Downloads, environment-triggered branches, and externally assembled payloads can reveal behavior absent from that context, motivating permission enforcement and execution-time monitoring alongside screening. The compact configuration’s timing does not measure the full Large-ID pipeline, and broker request decisions do not measure completed-task success. The eligible-subset false-positive increases under white-box rewrites and the limited valid adaptive-rewrite coverage also constrain deployment conclusions (Section 6.3).
